title: The new milestone Voyager 1 just crossed in interstellar space

blocks.text: Science

Voyager 1, already the farthest a human-made object has ever gone, has crossed the arbitrary but important threshold of a light day. It now takes 24 hours to send a message to the probe, now in interstellar space.
It took nearly 50 years to get to this point
It took nearly 50 years to get to where Voyager 1 is now. But it takes light just a day.
That's the new milestone — 16 billion miles, to be precise — the spacecraft has just reached.

“What it means is it takes a full day for light or radio signals from Earth to reach Voyager,” said Jason Rhodes, chief scientist for astrophysics, heliophysics and fundamental physics at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
“And it takes, of course, then another full day for the signals back from Voyager to reach Earth.”
It's not to scale, but Voyager 1 has come a long way in nearly 50 years. (CBC)

Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 was meant to study the gas giants of our solar system, Jupiter and Saturn. But by 1998, it continued on past them, becoming the farthest human-made object ever. It reached interstellar space — the region just outside the sun’s magnetic influence known as the heliopause — back in 2012, at a distance of 18 billion kilometres. Now, it’s more than 26 billion kilometres away.

“When we're talking about these scales, it really reminds us just how big space is,” said Bethany Downer, who works on the communications team for the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes, “and how impressive it is that something relatively small that we constructed is able to keep going indefinitely that way.”

blocks.text: Still working, talking

Arguably, being a “light day” away is an arbitrary threshold, as there’s no new physical boundary or change to Voyager 1 itself. But experts say it’s remarkable because it’s still plugging along on its mission while communicating with Earth.

“It's not operating, of course, as much as it used to be. There aren't as many instruments on board that are capturing science,” Downer said.

Voyager 1’s power is generated by the heat from the natural decay of plutonium. As that power has dwindled over nearly half a century, most of its science instruments have been shut down, the latest being the LCEP, which measured low-energy charged particles. There are two instruments that still work, one for measuring plasma waves and the other for magnetic fields.

“This tells us a lot about how stars form and how the distance between stars is not empty space, but filled with exciting particles and physics that we didn't really know about very well until Voyager,” Rhodes told CBC News from Pasadena, Calif.

Each of NASA's Voyager probes are equipped with three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs), including the one shown here. The RTGs provide power for the spacecraft by converting the heat generated by the decay of plutonium-238 into electricity. (NASA/JPL-Caltech)

Those instruments communicate to Earth via the deep space network, antennas located at multiple sites around the world dedicated to keeping continuous communication with spacecraft. Though Voyager 1’s signals are faint, it’s clear there’s a pretty big message we want to hear.
“Most important thing is: 'I'm still turned on, I'm still operating,'" Downer told CBC News from St. John’s.
Going but never gone

NASA expects Voyager 1 (and its sibling Voyager 2, launched the same year but on a different path) to continue being able to send messages for another decade, but Rhodes says there’s no definite endpoint as teams continue to work on energy-saving measures to try and extend it.
But even powerless, their missions won’t be over.
The special payload onboard both Voyager spacecraft, containing a snapshot of life and culture on Earth. (NASA/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)
“Both have a golden record,” Rhodes said, “and it's made of gold because that's a metal that won't tarnish or rust or decay.”

Effectively a time capsule, the golden records capture a cross-section of sounds from humanity, from greetings in 55 different languages to music to natural sounds of the earth, including thunder and humpback whales.
If you’re wondering how anyone might know how to play it, there are instructions. If you’re wondering who might play it, well, they’d have to think a little like us.

blocks.text: They also contain a message in Morse code, said Downer: "Ad astra per aspera," or "To the stars, through hardships."

While the long road continues for Voyager 1, it’s already provided deep insights into our solar system. Not least of which, an insight into ourselves, from this image taken in 1990 by Voyager 1 from six billion kilometres away.
The Pale Blue Dot is a photograph of Earth taken Feb. 14, 1990, by NASA’s Voyager 1 at a distance of 3.7 billion miles (6 billion kilometers) from the Sun. (NASA/JPL-Caltech)

Known as the Pale Blue Dot, it shows Earth as a tiny speck, bathed in a beam of light. Taken at the request of American astronomer Carl Sagan, he immortalized the significance of being so insignificant in his book of the same name.
“Consider again that dot. That’s here. That’s home. That’s us.”
